steps.title: Why we spend
steps.html:
One day a year, a small group of people stand in the busiest shops in the country and buy absolutely nothing. They think the rest of us should try it.

A  Every November the shops fill up. Prices fall, the windows say HALF-PRICE, and for a few days the whole country seems to be shopping. Some people queue outside the doors all night in the run-up to Christmas. Others buy on credit and only understand what they have spent when the bill arrives in January. In Britain alone, shoppers spend around nine billion pounds in that single week.

B  Then, on the busiest shopping day of the year, a small group of people stand in the same shopping centres holding signs. They are not buying anything. It is Buy Nothing Day, and they want the rest of us to stop for twenty-four hours and think. The movement started in Canada in 1992 and now appears in more than sixty-five countries.

C  “We believe shopping makes us happy,” says Lewis Castle, who has been part of the movement since 2013. “It doesn’t. Look at what happens afterwards.” He means the money people owe, and he means the planet: the richest fifth of the world’s population consumes far more than its fair share of the world’s resources, and moving goods around the world by air is one of the most harmful parts of the whole system.

D  Shops understand exactly how a bargain feels. A special offer does not simply mean a lower price; it means you were clever. Researchers who study consumer behaviour call this the deal effect, and it explains something strange: people come home with items they do not need, feel briefly pleased, and admit weeks later that they never wanted them at all. What follows has a plainer name. Guilt.

E  Guilt sells too. The current trend is guilt-free brands — a phone you can repair, a shirt made by workers who are paid properly, a coffee that promises to protect the forest it came from. Some shoppers are convinced this is real progress, and it is not hard to see why: a company that publishes what it pays its workers is doing something its competitors are not. Others think it is an excuse. Buy the guilt-free version, they argue, and you never have to ask the harder question.

F  That question is not what you buy. It is why. Castle does not tell anybody to stop shopping for ever, and he does not pretend that one day in November changes anything. He says something much smaller and, he thinks, more useful. For twenty-four hours, you notice how often your hand goes to your pocket — and you find out how much of it you actually wanted.
